strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: pretrained model selection for VLMs (composing a vision encoder + LLM + projector) is distinct from existing model-selection settings, and the paper is the first to systematically define it in this context.

Substantial experimental investment and rigor: the grid-search baseline exhaustively trains 49 candidates (~5439 GPU hours), providing reliable ground truth for evaluating search efficiency, and results are reported across six tasks in three domains.

Concrete, verifiable headline results: 8.9x-11.6x GPU-hour savings vs. grid search while finding the top-1 candidate on five of six tasks, plus weighted Kendall's tau ranking analysis, Top-5/Top-10 recovery analysis, component-wise ablations (Figure 10), sensitivity analysis (Table 5), and evaluation-time breakdown (Figure 11).

The two-axis design (reduce search space via two-step CKA-based clustering; reduce per-candidate cost via SHA early stopping and log-linear scaling prediction) is sensible, and the ablations show each component contributes; the observational scaling-law validation (Figure 9) supports the core assumption.

The discovered combinations (e.g., SigLIP-Vicuna, SigLIP-Llama) outperform the LLaVA-1.5-7B structure on the same alignment data, providing practical value; a usable API and implementation details (LoRA, FlashAttention, hyperparameters) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely a composition of established tools - CKA for representation similarity, Successive Halving for early stopping, and log-linear sample-scaling regression (already used for LLM selection, e.g., Lin et al. 2024). The main new contribution is applying them to the VLM alignment setting, plus the two-step clustering heuristic.

No empirical comparison against prior model selection methods. The paper argues (Section 2.3, Appendix E) that existing approaches fail for VLMs, but this claim is only asserted, not demonstrated. Even a best-effort adaptation of training-free proxies or random search would significantly strengthen the evaluation beyond the grid-search-only baseline.

Narrow experimental scope: only 7B-class LLMs, a single alignment dataset (LLaVA-1.5-Instruction), and six public benchmarks. The framework's core assumption - that a small sampled subset can predict full-data performance and that clusters transfer across tasks - is not stress-tested on realistic proprietary alignment data or on tasks where the scaling law is noisy.

One clear failure case is underexplored: on ChartQA Mordal selects a candidate scoring 18.6 vs. the grid-search best 20.2, yet the paper still reports 8.9x as a 'saving' with little discussion of when the method fails; the τ=0.52 result at tve=0.5 in the sensitivity analysis also indicates fragility to clustering thresholds.

Key hyperparameters (tve, tllm, top-k, R, u) appear task-dependent (harder tasks form many single-candidate clusters, inflating time), and the paper provides heuristics rather than principled guidance for choosing them; the claimed automation is therefore partially undermined.

Assumption of using held-out target benchmark data for ranking candidates during search is close to test-set tuning; the paper does not discuss validation-split protocol or potential overfitting of selection to the evaluation metric.
Clustering validity is supported with only four vision encoders on two datasets (Figure 8/Table 3), a small sample for a claim central to the search-space reduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practical problem: selecting pretrained vision encoders and LLMs to compose a VLM for a downstream task, which has received little dedicated attention; the empirical demonstration that no candidate combination dominates all tasks (Table 1) is a useful motivating observation.

The proposed pipeline is clearly described and reasonably engineered: two-step CKA-based clustering of vision encoders and LLMs, inter-/intra-cluster evaluation, SHA-based early stopping, and a log-linear 'observational scaling law' extrapolation to reduce per-candidate evaluation cost.

The evaluation is fairly extensive for a systems-style paper: a 49-candidate grid search ground truth across six benchmark datasets, ablations of each component, sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters, and an honest failure case discussion (ChartQA, where the selected candidate underperforms the true top-1).
The released interface and implementation details (LoRA-based finetuning, Flash Attention, bf16) improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Each component is a well-known technique applied in a new setting: CKA for representation similarity (Kornblith et al., 2019), successive halving (Jamieson & Talwalkar, 2016), and log-linear performance extrapolation with training data size (Lin et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024, which the authors themselves acknowledge). The core contribution is system integration rather than a new method, which may be insufficient for a top-tier AI conference without stronger insight or analysis.

The headline 8.9x–11.6x speedup is measured only against exhaustive grid search, which is a very weak baseline. There are no comparisons to obviously cheaper alternatives such as random search with early stopping, a single-stage SHA without clustering, or simply evaluating a small heuristic subset (e.g., the newest/largest models). Given SHA plus partial-data evaluation alone would likely yield a large fraction of the claimed speedup, the marginal value of the clustering machinery is unclear.

The search space is small and homogeneous: 7 vision encoders x 7 LLMs, all roughly 7B-scale, trained with one fixed alignment dataset (LLaVA-1.5-Instruction) and one projector architecture. The authors' own discussion (Appendix D) concedes the method may not extend to other model sizes, alignment schemes, or multi-user workloads, which substantially limits the significance and generality of the claims.

Selection reliability is imperfect and the cost of failures is not analyzed: the best candidate is found in only 5 of 6 tasks, and on ChartQA Mordal selects a candidate scoring 18.6 vs. 20.2 for the true top-1 (a meaningful gap). Several Top-5 candidates are missed (e.g., DINOv2-Vicuna on GQA). There is no analysis of when clustering thresholds cause strong candidates to be discarded, and no repeated runs or variance estimates to support the reported τ values and times.

The 'observational scaling law' claim is weakly supported: Figure 9 shows log-linear error trends for only five VLMs on two datasets, fitted over a narrow sample range (2^13–2^18 samples). Extrapolating from 1/8 of the data to full-data performance via a linear fit in log-log space is a strong assumption whose error bound is never quantified; prediction error at r=1 is not reported.

Several important experimental details are underspecified for reproducibility: how the medoid/representative selection interacts with warm-started projectors, the exact definition of 'warmed-up feature projector' used for LLM clustering, and how grid-search training used for the ground truth matches Mordal's truncated training procedure. Typos and notation issues (e.g., inconsistent δ = 5e−5 vs. 0.01 in Listing 1, Algorithm 1's p/δ semantics) further hurt clarity.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: automated pretrained model selection for VLMs is a practical and timely challenge, and the paper is (to my knowledge) among the first to formalize it in the VLM/alignment setting, where existing zero-shot or LLM-only selection methods genuinely fail.

The design is sensible and well-decomposed along two orthogonal axes (reducing the search space via CKA-based two-step clustering, and reducing per-candidate evaluation cost via SHA early stopping and an observational scaling law). Each component is validated separately in ablations (Figure 10).

Substantial experimental effort: a full grid search over 49 VLM candidates (7 encoders × 7 LLMs) across six benchmark datasets, costing 5000+ GPU hours, provides a strong ground-truth baseline and enables honest measurement of both speedup and ranking fidelity (Kendall's τ).

Good methodological hygiene: the observational scaling law for VLM alignment is empirically validated (Figure 9), sensitivity analyses for the clustering thresholds and top-k parameters are provided (Appendix C.2), and implementation details (LoRA, FlashAttention, hyperparameters, interface) support reproducibility.

Practical takeaway for practitioners: discovered model combinations (e.g., SigLIP-Vicuna, SigLIP-Llama, SigLIP-Qwen) that outperform the LLaVA-1.5 structure on several tasks, demonstrating that the 'no silver bullet' claim has actionable value.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the three ingredients (CKA representation similarity, Successive Halving, and log-linear scaling-law extrapolation) are all established techniques; the contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation to the VLM alignment setting rather than a new method.

The headline speedup (8.9×–11.6×) is largely an artifact of the small, fixed 49-candidate grid; the only baseline is exhaustive grid search. There is no comparison against cheaper and equally obvious baselines such as random search, greedy search over one modality at a time, or adapted transferability estimators (e.g., LogME variants), which could plausibly achieve similar savings and are needed to establish Mordal's relative value.

Consistency issue in Table 2: on ChartQA, grid search's top-1 achieves 20.2 while Mordal selects a model with 18.6, i.e., Mordal fails to find the true best model on one of six tasks, yet this failure is not explicitly analyzed or discussed alongside the 'five out of six' claim.

Narrow scope of the search space: all LLMs are 7B-scale and all encoders are ViT/ConvNeXt-scale; the authors themselves acknowledge (Appendix D) that similarity measures and the scaling law may not transfer to different model sizes, limiting the generality of the central claims.

Key hyperparameters (t_ve = 0.7, t_llm = 0.8, top_k, η, R) appear hand-tuned on the same tasks used for evaluation; sensitivity analysis shows τ can degrade sharply (0.52 at t_ve = 0.5), so robustness of the defaults on unseen tasks remains an open question.

Generalization of the clustering hypothesis is only validated with four vision encoders on two datasets (Figure 8/Table 3), a small sample; a more systematic correlation study between CKA similarity and post-alignment performance gaps would strengthen the core assumption.

Alignment is fixed to the LLaVA-1.5-Instruction recipe with a specific projector; whether conclusions hold for other alignment data, training budgets, or VLM families (e.g., cross-attention or native-resolution architectures like Qwen2-VL-style designs) is untested.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: pretrained component selection for LLM-based VLMs is practically important, and the paper convincingly demonstrates (Table 1, Appendix A) that no single pretrained combination dominates across tasks and that fine-tuning does not eliminate these differences.

The framework addresses cost reduction along two complementary and clearly articulated dimensions (number of candidates via CKA-based two-step clustering with inter-/intra-cluster evaluation, and per-candidate cost via SHA early stopping and observational scaling-law prediction), with sensible co-design (checkpoint reuse).

Extensive empirical evaluation: 49-candidate grid search ground truth across seven datasets spanning multiple task types, comparisons against four transferability baselines (EMMS, LogME, LEEP, NLEEP) under matched compute budgets, ablation studies (Figure 7), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Table 4), compute-time breakdown (Figure 8), and additional studies on smaller LLMs (D.3), training-free regimes (D.4), and Q-former projectors (D.5).

Strong headline results: finds the top-1 VLM in 6/7 tasks with ~9–11.6x fewer GPU hours than grid search, and substantially higher weighted Kendall's tau than existing model-selection methods on all seven datasets.

Honest discussion of limitations (missing top-1 on ChartQA, sensitivity to clustering thresholds, degraded reliability on smaller models) and a detailed, reproducibility-oriented appendix with algorithms and the model zoo.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: each component is an adaptation of well-known techniques (CKA for representation similarity, Successive Halving for early stopping, log-linear extrapolation of loss vs. data size for scaling prediction). The contribution is primarily their combination and application to the VLM alignment setting rather than a new method or theory.

Evaluation scale is modest relative to the motivating claims: the search space is only 7x7=49 curated candidates, while the introduction motivates the problem with the '150,000+ models on HuggingFace' ecosystem. Experiments are confined to ~7B LLMs, MLP projectors, and a single alignment dataset (LLaVA-1.5); generality beyond this setting is untested or acknowledged as problematic (small models in D.3 show noticeably lower tau).

The primary speedup baseline (grid search) is a weak naive baseline; ~500 GPU hours per task for Mordal remains a substantial cost, and no comparison is made against more recent learning-based model-selection approaches (e.g., LensLLM, which is cited but not compared) or alternative pruning strategies such as random search under the same budget.

The clustering step introduces a real risk of irrecoverable errors (the best candidate eliminated in 1/7 tasks, tau dropping to 0.52 for tve=0.5 in Table 4), and the paper offers no principled way to set thresholds tve/tllm — results appear sensitive to hyperparameters that users would need to tune.

The 'observational scaling law' is empirically fitted per candidate with only a few points and a linear regression in log-log space; the paper provides limited analysis of when this extrapolation fails (beyond noting small-model instability), and the log-linear regime only emerges after a certain number of samples, which partly undermines the cost savings.
Reproducibility is promised but the code/checkpoints are stated to be released 'in the future'; as submitted, results could not be independently verified.

strengths: Addresses a real and timely problem: selecting pretrained vision encoders and LLMs for task-specific VLMs, where no single off-the-shelf VLM dominates all benchmarks (motivated convincingly by Figure 1 and Table 1).

The empirical motivation is thorough: a full 49-candidate grid search provides ground-truth rankings, and the paper demonstrates that (a) no silver-bullet pretrained combination exists and (b) task-specific fine-tuning does not eliminate performance differences (Appendix A), which strengthens the case for the problem itself.

The framing of the search problem along two orthogonal axes (reducing the number of candidates via CKA-based clustering, and reducing per-candidate evaluation cost via SHA early stopping and scaling-law-based prediction) is sensible and clearly explained, with a complete algorithm (Algorithm 2) and pseudocode.

The experimental coverage is broad: seven tasks across three domains, four transferability baselines (EMMS, LogME, LEEP, NLEEP) under matched compute budgets, ablations of each component (Figure 7), sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters (Table 4), plus additional studies on small-scale models, training-free settings, and Q-former projectors in the appendix.

The paper is honest about failure modes: it reports the ChartQA case where Mordal misses the top-1 model and regresses in top-1 score, discusses premature exclusion by early stopping, and openly lists limitations in Appendix E.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. Each component is an existing technique applied in a new setting: CKA for representation similarity (Kornblith et al., 2019), Successive Halving for early stopping (Jamieson & Talwalkar, 2016), and log-linear performance extrapolation over data size (Lin et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024). The contribution is primarily an engineering integration and a system, which may be below the novelty bar for a top-tier AI conference.

Limited scale and generality of the search space. The evaluation uses only a 7×7 model zoo with 7B LLMs and a single fixed alignment dataset (LLaVA-1.5-Instruction). Given the paper's own motivation of 'over 150,000 LLMs on HuggingFace', the demonstrated search space is tiny, and it is unclear how clustering quality and threshold selection (tve, tllm) would behave at realistic zoo sizes. Appendix D.3 further shows the approach degrades for smaller models.

The sensitivity analysis reveals meaningful fragility: the clustering threshold tve changes weighted Kendall's τ from 0.52 to 0.86 and search time from 446 to 1041 GPU hours. Tuning these thresholds per task appears necessary, undermining the 'without manual intervention' claim, and no principled method for choosing thresholds is provided.

The absolute cost savings are less compelling than the headline speedup: Mordal still consumes roughly 470-610 GPU hours per task. For a practitioner, a 10× reduction from 5439 GPU hours on a 49-model zoo may still be prohibitive, and the framework does not exploit cross-task or cross-user reuse (acknowledged only as future work).

The comparison with transferability baselines, while run under matched budgets, is arguably a setup where those baselines are known to fail (they were not designed for alignment-dependent VLMs); a stronger competitive reference, such as direct few-shot alignment evaluation or a simple random-subset training policy, is missing.

Several results are supported only on two datasets (GQA and AI2D): the observational scaling law validation (Figure 7a/7b) and the ablations of early stopping vs. scaling prediction (Figure 7c/7d). Given that the log-linear trend emerges only above a certain sample count, its validity across harder tasks like ChartQA/DocVQA is not established.

Reproducibility is not yet demonstrated: code, checkpoints, and evaluation results are only promised 'in the future', so none of the 5439 GPU-hour ground-truth rankings or the framework itself can currently be verified independently.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: automated selection of pretrained vision encoders and LLMs for VLM construction is a practical, timely gap, and the paper convincingly shows (Table 1, Appendix A) that no off-the-shelf VLM contains the best components for every task, even after fine-tuning.

Unusually thorough empirical grounding: the authors actually trained a 7x7 grid of 49 VLM candidates (5,439 GPU hours) per task to establish ground truth, which is far beyond what most model-selection papers do, making the Kendall's tau comparisons meaningful.

Comprehensive evaluation: seven diverse tasks (including MMMU), fair compute-matched comparison against four transferability baselines (EMMS, LogME, LEEP, NLEEP), ablations of every component (EE/ES/SP), sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters, and useful appendix studies (small-scale models, training-free regime, Q-former projectors, time breakdown).

Strong headline results: ~9-12x GPU-hour savings over grid search while recovering the top-1 model in 6/7 tasks, and consistently higher weighted Kendall's tau than all baselines; the top selected VLMs also beat the default LLaVA-1.5 configuration.
Honest self-assessment: the paper openly discusses failure cases (ChartQA top-1 miss, hyperparameter sensitivity, degraded scaling prediction on small models) in the limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the individual components are all well-established (CKA for representation similarity, Successive Halving for early stopping, log-linear scaling laws for performance extrapolation, hierarchical clustering). The contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination applied to a new setting rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Single alignment dataset: all searches use the LLaVA-1.5-Instruction mixture. Given the paper's claim of task-specific selection, it is unclear how sensitive the rankings and clustering structure are to a different alignment corpus; generalization across alignment data is untested.

Small, curated search space: only 7 vision encoders and 7 similar-sized (7B-class) LLMs. The motivation invokes 150,000+ HuggingFace models, but the framework's behavior and cost on a much larger, more heterogeneous zoo (different scales, quantized models, multitask models) is unverified.

Dependence on training configuration: selection is performed under one specific recipe (MLP projector, LoRA, fixed hyperparameters). Whether the identified 'best' pretrained combination transfers to other training setups (full fine-tuning, different projectors, different LoRA ranks) is not demonstrated, and the Q-former study is only small-scale.

Sensitivity to clustering thresholds is substantial: e.g., t_ve=0.5 drops Kendall's tau to 0.52 and t_ve=0.9 costs 2x search time, and the paper admits hyperparameter balancing is crucial; an automated or adaptive thresholding mechanism is left as future work.

Results are based on single runs with no variance or seed reporting, so differences of a few tenths in tau or a point in accuracy are hard to interpret; the metric (ranking correlation against a single grid-search ranking) is also noisy.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code and checkpoints are only promised 'in the future', and several implementation details (e.g., exact checkpoint reuse during scaling prediction, GPU allocation policy) are described at a high level only.

The 69% improvement claim over 'state-of-the-art' rests mostly on transferability baselines (EMMS/LogME/LEEP/NLEEP) that the authors themselves argue are fundamentally ill-suited to VLMs, making that comparison somewhat expected; no stronger alignment-aware selection baseline is compared.
